listen.title: A Change of Appointment
listen.text: Hi, this is Laura calling from Brookside Dental Practice, and this message is for Mister Weber. I'm calling about your appointment on Thursday at half past ten. Unfortunately, Doctor Hayes has been called away to a training course that day, so we're having to move a few patients around. I'm really sorry about that. Now, we've got two options for you. There's a slot on Wednesday afternoon at a quarter past four, or, if that's too soon, we could see you next Monday first thing, at eight o'clock. The Monday appointment would be with Doctor Hayes herself, whereas on Wednesday you'd be seeing her colleague, Doctor Patel, who's also very experienced. Oh, and since this is your yearly check-up, please remember to bring the new insurance card you mentioned last time, because the old one won't be accepted anymore. Could you give us a ring back before Tuesday lunchtime? Otherwise, I'm afraid we might have to give both slots away. Our number is oh one six three, four nine two, seven seven eight. Thanks, and have a lovely day.

questions.q: What is the main purpose of the message?
options: To cancel all appointments at the practice
To offer new times for a postponed appointment
To remind the patient of an unpaid bill
To introduce a new dentist at the practice
questions.answer: To offer new times for a postponed appointment
questions.explain_de: Der Termin fällt aus und Laura bietet zwei Ersatztermine an.

questions.q: Why can't Doctor Hayes see the patient on Thursday?
options: She is ill
She is on holiday
She is attending a training course
She has an emergency patient
questions.answer: She is attending a training course
questions.explain_de: Sie wurde zu einer Fortbildung („training course“) gerufen.

questions.q: What should the patient bring?
options: His old insurance card
A letter from his doctor
His new insurance card
A list of his medication
questions.answer: His new insurance card
questions.explain_de: Die alte Karte wird nicht mehr akzeptiert, er soll die neue mitbringen.

questions.q: If the patient wants to see Doctor Hayes, what will he probably do?
options: Choose the Wednesday slot
Keep the Thursday appointment
Choose the Monday slot
Wait until Tuesday lunchtime to decide
questions.answer: Choose the Monday slot
questions.explain_de: Nur der Montagstermin ist bei Doctor Hayes selbst; mittwochs behandelt Doctor Patel.

listen.title: Why We Sleep Badly
listen.text: Welcome back to Everyday Science. So, today's question comes from a listener who says she's exhausted every morning, even though she's in bed by eleven. And honestly, she's not alone. Researchers who looked at around two thousand adults found that nearly half of them felt tired most days. Now, the usual suspect is the phone, right? Scrolling in bed. And yes, screens do play a part, but interestingly, the study suggests it's not mainly the light. It's the content. If you're reading work emails or arguing with someone online, your brain simply doesn't switch off. Watching a calm nature documentary, on the other hand, seems to do very little harm. The other big factor was irregular timing. People who went to bed at wildly different times at the weekend slept worse during the week, almost like a mini jet lag. So what's the advice? Well, keep your bedtime roughly the same, even on Saturdays, and if you really can't leave the phone alone, at least avoid anything stressful in the last hour. Small changes, but they seem to add up.

questions.q: What is the episode mainly about?
options: How phones damage your eyes
Reasons for poor sleep and simple ways to improve it
Why adults need more sleep than children
The health risks of jet lag
questions.answer: Reasons for poor sleep and simple ways to improve it
questions.explain_de: Es geht um Ursachen von schlechtem Schlaf (Inhalte, unregelmäßige Zeiten) und Tipps.

questions.q: According to the study, what is the main problem with using phones in bed?
options: The bright light
The stressful content
The noise of notifications
The time spent charging
questions.answer: The stressful content
questions.explain_de: Die Studie sagt: nicht hauptsächlich das Licht, sondern der Inhalt.

questions.q: How many adults felt tired most days?
options: About two thousand
Nearly a quarter
Nearly half
Almost all of them
questions.answer: Nearly half
questions.explain_de: „nearly half of them felt tired most days“.

questions.q: What would the presenter probably say about watching a relaxing film in bed?
options: It is probably fine
It is the worst habit of all
It causes a kind of jet lag
It should be replaced by reading emails
questions.answer: It is probably fine
questions.explain_de: Eine ruhige Naturdoku schadet laut Sendung kaum – ein entspannender Film also wohl auch nicht.

listen.title: The Bike Lane Debate
listen.text: And now to local news. The city council has finally approved the new cycle lane along Harbour Road, after almost two years of discussion. Work is due to start in March and should take about five months. The plan will remove around sixty parking spaces, which is why local shop owners have been so strongly against it. Many of them argue that customers who drive in from nearby villages simply won't come anymore. The council, however, points to a trial in the town of Millbridge, where a similar lane was introduced three years ago. There, shop owners were also worried at first, but footfall actually went up by roughly twelve percent, mainly because more people began cycling and walking into the centre. To calm things down, the council has promised a new car park on the edge of town, with a free shuttle bus every fifteen minutes. Whether that'll be ready in time is another question. The first phase of the car park isn't expected to open until next autumn.

questions.q: What is the report mainly about?
options: A new car park opening in March
The approval of a controversial cycle lane
Shops closing in the town centre
A bus service to nearby villages
questions.answer: The approval of a controversial cycle lane
questions.explain_de: Der Stadtrat hat den umstrittenen Radweg genehmigt.

questions.q: Why are shop owners against the plan?
options: Construction will take two years
Parking spaces will be removed
The shuttle bus will be too expensive
Cyclists rarely buy anything
questions.answer: Parking spaces will be removed
questions.explain_de: Rund sechzig Parkplätze fallen weg, deshalb fürchten sie weniger Kunden.

questions.q: What happened in Millbridge?
options: Shops lost about twelve percent of customers
The cycle lane was removed after three years
The number of visitors to shops increased
A free shuttle bus was introduced
questions.answer: The number of visitors to shops increased
questions.explain_de: „footfall actually went up by roughly twelve percent“.

questions.q: What does the reporter suggest about the new car park?
options: It may not be ready when the cycle lane is finished
It will be larger than planned
It has already been cancelled
It will replace the shuttle bus
questions.answer: It may not be ready when the cycle lane is finished
questions.explain_de: Der Radweg ist nach ca. fünf Monaten fertig, der Parkplatz öffnet erst nächsten Herbst.

listen.title: Release Date Check-in
listen.text: Okay, let's get started, because I know a few of you have a hard stop at eleven. So, the big item today is the release of the new mobile scanning feature. As you know, we were aiming for the fifteenth of next month. The honest update is that we're not going to make that. During testing, the team found that scanned invoices sometimes lose their metadata when the connection drops halfway through an upload. It doesn't happen often, but if it hits a customer's accounting documents, that's a serious problem, and frankly, not something we want to ship. Priya's team reckons they need another two weeks to fix it properly and then a week of regression testing. So realistically, we're looking at the fifth of the month after. What I'd like from sales is a heads-up on any customers who've been promised the earlier date, because I'd rather we call them ourselves than have them find out from the release notes. And marketing, can we hold off on the announcement for now?

questions.q: What is the main message of the meeting?
options: The scanning feature has been cancelled
The release is delayed because of a quality problem
Sales has promised too many new features
Marketing has already announced the release
questions.answer: The release is delayed because of a quality problem
questions.explain_de: Wegen eines Fehlers beim Upload wird der Release verschoben.

questions.q: When does the bug occur?
options: When invoices are very large
When the connection is lost during an upload
When several users scan at the same time
When documents are exported to accounting software
questions.answer: When the connection is lost during an upload
questions.explain_de: „when the connection drops halfway through an upload“.

questions.q: How much extra time does the team need in total?
options: One week
Two weeks
Three weeks
Five weeks
questions.answer: Three weeks
questions.explain_de: Zwei Wochen Fix plus eine Woche Regressionstests.

questions.q: Why does the speaker want sales to name certain customers?
options: So those customers can test the feature early
So the company can inform them personally before they read about it
So marketing can use them in the announcement
So the customers can be offered a discount
questions.answer: So the company can inform them personally before they read about it
questions.explain_de: Er will sie lieber selbst anrufen, als dass sie es aus den Release Notes erfahren.

vocab.de: ein fester Endtermin (man muss pünktlich gehen)

listen.title: Onboarding a New Customer
listen.text: Right, quick briefing on Fairfield Logistics before tomorrow's kick-off call. They're a mid-sized company, about a hundred and forty employees, and they've been storing everything on an old file server plus, well, a lot of paper. They've signed up for our cloud plan, starting with the finance and HR departments. Now, a couple of things to watch out for. First, their IT manager, Tom, is quite sceptical. He wasn't the one who chose us, the managing director was, so expect a lot of questions about data security and where the servers are located. Make sure you mention that everything's hosted in Frankfurt. Second, they want the HR files migrated first, which is the more sensitive data, so we'll need to agree access rights before we move a single document. My suggestion is that we don't overload them. Let's aim for a pilot with around twenty users in the first month, get some quick wins, and only then roll it out to the whole finance team. Any questions before we wrap up?

questions.q: What is the purpose of this briefing?
options: To prepare the team for a first meeting with a new customer
To explain why a customer cancelled their contract
To train the customer's IT manager
To present the results of a pilot project
questions.answer: To prepare the team for a first meeting with a new customer
questions.explain_de: Es ist ein kurzes Briefing vor dem Kick-off-Call am nächsten Tag.

questions.q: Which department's files will be migrated first?
options: Finance
HR
IT
Logistics
questions.answer: HR
questions.explain_de: „they want the HR files migrated first“.

questions.q: How many users should take part in the pilot?
options: About fourteen
About twenty
About forty
About a hundred and forty
questions.answer: About twenty
questions.explain_de: „a pilot with around twenty users in the first month“.

questions.q: Why is Tom probably sceptical?
options: He had a bad experience with cloud software before
He was not involved in choosing the supplier
He thinks the product is too expensive
He wants to keep using paper files
questions.answer: He was not involved in choosing the supplier
questions.explain_de: Der Geschäftsführer hat entschieden, nicht Tom – daher wohl seine Skepsis.

listen.title: A Partner Wants Better Terms
listen.text: Hi Markus, it's Sarah from Northgate Systems. Sorry I missed you, I guess you're in back-to-back meetings. Anyway, I wanted to follow up on the partner pricing you sent over last week. So, overall we're really keen to add your cloud product to our portfolio, and our customers have been asking for something like this. The thing is, the twenty percent partner margin is a bit lower than what we're getting from other vendors. Most of them are closer to twenty-five. I'm not saying that's a deal-breaker, but it does make it harder for me to get sign-off internally. One idea we had was a tiered model, so maybe twenty percent to begin with and then more once we hit a certain number of customers, say thirty in the first year. That way you're not taking a big risk upfront. Also, could you check whether you'd cover the cost of training for our sales people? Give me a call when you get a chance. I'm around all afternoon, except between two and three.

questions.q: Why is Sarah calling?
options: To cancel the partnership
To discuss and negotiate the partner pricing
To order training for her customers
To complain about a delayed delivery
questions.answer: To discuss and negotiate the partner pricing
questions.explain_de: Sie reagiert auf das Preisangebot und schlägt andere Konditionen vor.

questions.q: What margin do other vendors usually offer, according to Sarah?
options: About twenty percent
About twenty-five percent
About thirty percent
About fifteen percent
questions.answer: About twenty-five percent
questions.explain_de: „Most of them are closer to twenty-five.“

questions.q: What does Sarah suggest?
options: A fixed margin of twenty-five percent from the start
A margin that increases after reaching a customer target
Free licences for the first thirty customers
A shorter contract of one year
questions.answer: A margin that increases after reaching a customer target
questions.explain_de: Ein gestaffeltes Modell: mehr Marge ab z. B. dreißig Kunden.

questions.q: What can we infer about Sarah's position?
options: She will not sign unless she gets twenty-five percent
She wants the deal but needs better terms to convince her company
She has already got internal approval
She prefers another vendor's product
questions.answer: She wants the deal but needs better terms to convince her company
questions.explain_de: Sie ist „keen“, sagt aber, 20 % machen die interne Freigabe schwerer – kein Deal-Breaker.

listen.title: Debrief After the Negotiation
listen.text: So, how did it go? Well, mixed, to be honest. On the plus side, they've more or less accepted our pricing, which, given how hard they pushed back in the first round, I didn't see coming. What they're not budging on is the service level agreement. They want guaranteed availability of ninety-nine point nine percent, with penalties if we fall short, and legal won't sign off on penalties of that size. My sense is that the pricing concession was a bit of a tactical move. They gave ground there so they could dig their heels in on the contract terms, and I think we underestimated how much their procurement team is being driven by a bad experience with a previous supplier. So rather than going back with a flat no, I'd suggest we reframe it. We could offer the ninety-nine point nine as a target, but cap the penalties at, say, one month's fees, and throw in quarterly service reviews. That addresses the underlying concern, which is really about trust, without exposing us to unlimited risk.

questions.q: What is the overall outcome of the negotiation so far?
options: A complete agreement on all points
Progress on price but a sticking point on contract terms
A breakdown of talks over pricing
An agreement on penalties but not on price
questions.answer: Progress on price but a sticking point on contract terms
questions.explain_de: Preise sind fast akzeptiert, beim SLA gibt es keine Einigung.

questions.q: Why won't the speaker's company agree to the customer's demand?
options: The availability target is technically impossible
The legal team won't accept penalties that large
The price would become too low
The customer wants monthly service reviews
questions.answer: The legal team won't accept penalties that large
questions.explain_de: „legal won't sign off on penalties of that size“.

questions.q: What does the speaker propose to limit the penalties?
options: A maximum of one month's fees
A maximum of one quarter's fees
No penalties at all
Penalties only after a year
questions.answer: A maximum of one month's fees
questions.explain_de: „cap the penalties at, say, one month's fees“.

questions.q: What does the speaker believe is really behind the customer's demands?
options: They want to lower the price even further
They are looking for a reason to walk away
They lack trust because of problems with a former supplier
Their legal team is inexperienced
questions.answer: They lack trust because of problems with a former supplier
questions.explain_de: Er vermutet schlechte Erfahrungen mit einem früheren Anbieter; das eigentliche Thema sei Vertrauen.

vocab.de: sich querstellen, auf seiner Position beharren

listen.title: Where to Focus in Year One
listen.text: Let me frame the decision we need to make today. We've got the cloud product ready, and broadly speaking there are two ways to take it to market. Option one is to go wide, targeting small businesses across every sector with a low monthly price and a self-service sign-up. The appeal is obvious, but the churn rates in that segment tend to be brutal, and our brand isn't well known outside the enterprise space. Option two is to go narrow, picking two verticals where we already have credibility, say tax advisers and mid-sized manufacturers, and building templates and integrations specifically for them. It's slower, admittedly, and it means turning down some opportunities in the short term. But the data from our pilot is fairly telling. Customers who came in through a partner in one of those verticals were three times as likely to still be active after six months. So, my recommendation is option two for the first twelve months, with a clear review point, rather than spreading ourselves too thin before we've proven the model.

questions.q: What is the speaker mainly doing?
options: Reporting the final results of the product launch
Presenting two market strategies and recommending one
Explaining how the pilot was organised
Announcing a price reduction for small businesses
questions.answer: Presenting two market strategies and recommending one
questions.explain_de: Sie stellt zwei Go-to-Market-Optionen vor und empfiehlt Option zwei.

questions.q: What is a disadvantage of targeting all small businesses?
options: The product is not ready yet
Many customers tend to cancel quickly
Partners refuse to sell it
Integrations would be too expensive
questions.answer: Many customers tend to cancel quickly
questions.explain_de: „churn rates in that segment tend to be brutal“ – hohe Abwanderung.

questions.q: What did the pilot data show?
options: Self-service customers stayed longer
Partner customers in the two sectors were more likely to remain active
Manufacturers were three times cheaper to acquire
Tax advisers preferred a low monthly price
questions.answer: Partner customers in the two sectors were more likely to remain active
questions.explain_de: Sie waren nach sechs Monaten dreimal so häufig noch aktiv.

questions.q: What does the speaker imply about the broad strategy?
options: It should never be considered
It might be reconsidered once the focused approach has proven itself
It was more successful in the pilot
It has already been rejected by the board
questions.answer: It might be reconsidered once the focused approach has proven itself
questions.explain_de: Sie spricht von einem klaren Review-Punkt und davon, sich nicht zu verzetteln, „bevor“ das Modell bewiesen ist.

without having to worry about…

write.task_de: Ein Kunde beschwert sich, dass sein Team gestern zwei Stunden nicht auf Dokumente zugreifen konnte. Schreibe eine formelle Antwort: Problem anerkennen, Ursache erklären, Maßnahmen nennen und eine Kulanzgeste anbieten.

write.task_de: Schreibe eine Nachricht an die Marketingleiterin (gleiche Ebene) und argumentiere, dass sich der Cloud-Launch auf zwei Branchen statt auf alle KMU konzentrieren sollte. Nimm einen Einwand vorweg und entkräfte ihn.

articles.title: Why Keeping Customers Matters More Than Winning New Ones
articles.teaser: For software companies that sell subscriptions, the real work starts after the contract is signed.
articles.text:
When people imagine a successful software company, they often picture a sales team celebrating a big new deal. For companies that sell software as a subscription, however, that moment is only the beginning. The contract might last a year or even just a month, and the customer can walk away at the next renewal date. This is why many subscription businesses now treat customer retention as their most important goal.

The reason is simple economics. Winning a new customer is expensive. Marketing campaigns, sales calls, product demos and free trials all cost money, and it can take many months before a customer has paid enough to cover these costs. If that customer cancels after a short time, the company actually loses money on the deal. On the other hand, a customer who stays for several years becomes more profitable every month, because the cost of serving them is usually much lower than the cost of finding them in the first place.

Experts often describe the problem as a "leaky bucket". Imagine pouring water into a bucket with holes in it. You can pour faster and faster, but if the water keeps running out, the bucket never fills up. In the same way, a company with high churn – the share of customers who cancel – has to keep growing its sales just to stand still. Reducing churn, even slightly, can have a surprisingly large effect on long-term growth.

So how do companies keep their customers? The first step usually happens right after the sale, during onboarding. If new users struggle to set up the product or do not see its value quickly, they are much more likely to leave. That is why many companies offer guided setup, training sessions and simple checklists. Many also build dedicated customer success teams. Unlike traditional support staff, who react to problems, these teams contact customers proactively, check how the product is being used and suggest ways to get more out of it.

Data plays a big role, too. Modern software can show which features customers use and how often they log in. A sudden drop in activity is often an early warning sign that a customer is unhappy or has found an alternative. By spotting these signals early, a company has a chance to fix the problem before the renewal date arrives.

Finally, loyal customers bring benefits that are hard to measure. They are more likely to upgrade to more expensive plans, buy additional features and recommend the product to others. For a small or medium-sized business choosing new software, a recommendation from a satisfied peer is often worth more than any advertisement. In the subscription world, a happy customer is not just revenue – it is also the best marketing a company can have.
keypoints: In subscription software, customers can cancel at every renewal, so retention is a key goal.
Winning new customers is expensive, and a customer only becomes profitable if they stay long enough.
High churn is like a leaky bucket: the company must sell more just to stay at the same size.
Good onboarding, proactive customer success teams and usage data help companies keep customers.
Loyal customers upgrade, buy more and recommend the product, which brings extra growth.

articles.title: Selling Through Others: How Partner Channels Really Work
articles.teaser: Some software companies reach thousands of customers without ever meeting most of them – here is how they pull it off.
articles.text:
For a software vendor with ambitious growth targets, there is only so much a direct sales team can achieve. Every salesperson has a limited number of hours, a limited territory and a limited network. Sooner or later, many companies come to the same conclusion: if you want to scale, you need other people to sell on your behalf. This is the basic idea behind a partner channel.

Partners come in several shapes and sizes. Resellers buy the software, or licences for it, and sell it on to their own customers, often bundled with hardware or other products. System integrators and consultancies focus on implementation, tailoring the software to a client's processes and connecting it to existing systems. Referral partners, by contrast, simply recommend the product and receive a fee for every deal that closes. What they all have in common is something the vendor usually lacks: established relationships and, crucially, the trust of local businesses.

That trust is particularly valuable when the target market consists of small and medium-sized enterprises. A family-owned manufacturer is unlikely to respond to a cold email from an unknown software company, yet it may well follow the advice of the IT service provider that has looked after its servers for fifteen years. In this sense, partners do not merely widen a vendor's reach; they lend it credibility it could hardly build on its own.

None of this comes for free, of course. Partners expect a healthy margin, and the vendor inevitably gives up a degree of control over how its product is positioned, priced and supported. Channel conflict is another notorious pitfall. If the direct sales team and a partner end up chasing the same customer, relationships can turn sour remarkably quickly. Well-run programmes therefore draw clear lines, for example by reserving certain regions or customer sizes for partners, and by registering deals so that nobody is undercut at the last minute.

The shift towards cloud products has also changed the game. When software was installed on premises, partners earned much of their income from one-off installation projects. With subscription models, revenue trickles in month by month, and implementation is often lighter. Smart vendors respond by rewarding partners for long-term customer success rather than just the initial sale – through recurring commissions, for instance, or by paying for services such as training and data migration.

Ultimately, a partner channel stands or falls on whether partners genuinely want to sell the product. Glossy brochures and an attractive discount are rarely enough. Partners need thorough training, easy access to demo systems, marketing support and a contact person who actually answers the phone. Treat them as an afterthought, and they will quietly push a competitor's solution instead. Treat them as an extension of your own team, and they can become the engine of growth that no direct sales force could match.
keypoints: Direct sales teams have limits, so companies use partners to sell on their behalf and grow faster.
There are different partner types, such as resellers, system integrators and referral partners.
Partners bring existing relationships and trust, which is especially important when selling to SMEs.
Partner channels have costs and risks, including margins, less control and conflict with direct sales.
Cloud subscriptions change partner income, and success depends on training, support and treating partners as part of the team.

articles.title: Your New Colleague Is an Algorithm
articles.teaser: AI assistants are arriving in offices everywhere, but using them well is a skill people still need to learn.
articles.text:
Only a few years ago, artificial intelligence at work sounded like science fiction. Today, many office workers use AI tools every day, often without thinking much about it. They ask a chatbot to write the first draft of an email, summarise a long report or translate a document. For many people, AI has quietly become a new kind of colleague. But what does this colleague do well, and where does it still need supervision?

The biggest benefit is speed. Tasks that used to take an hour, such as turning meeting notes into a clear summary, can now take a few minutes. AI is especially good at repetitive work with text: sorting incoming documents, pulling key information out of invoices or suggesting answers to common customer questions. This gives employees more time for work that needs human judgement, like building relationships with customers or making difficult decisions.

However, AI tools also make mistakes, and they often make them with great confidence. A chatbot can produce a sentence that sounds perfectly professional but contains wrong facts, invented sources or numbers that do not add up. Experts call this "hallucination". For this reason, many companies tell their staff to treat AI output as a starting point, not a finished product. A human should always check the result before it is sent to a customer or used for an important decision.

There are also questions about data protection. When employees paste confidential information into a public AI tool, they may not know where that data ends up. In Europe, where privacy rules are strict, this is a serious concern. As a result, many organisations now create clear guidelines: which tools are allowed, what kind of information can be shared and who is responsible for the final result. Some companies prefer AI features built directly into the software they already use, so that sensitive data stays in a controlled environment.

Perhaps the most interesting change is in the skills people need. Writing a good instruction for an AI – often called a "prompt" – is a bit like briefing a new intern. You have to explain the context, describe the goal and say what the result should look like. People who can do this clearly tend to get much better results. At the same time, classic skills like critical thinking and good writing become more important, not less, because someone has to judge whether the AI's work is actually good.

In the end, AI is unlikely to replace most office jobs completely, at least not soon. But it is changing them. The workers who benefit most will probably be those who learn to work alongside the technology: using it for the boring parts, checking its work carefully and keeping the important decisions in human hands.
keypoints: Many office workers already use AI tools daily for tasks like drafting, summarising and translating.
The main benefit is speed on repetitive text tasks, which frees time for work needing human judgement.
AI can make confident mistakes (hallucinations), so humans must check its output.
Data protection is a concern, so companies create guidelines about which tools and data are allowed.
New skills like writing good prompts matter, and critical thinking becomes more important, not less.

articles.title: From Gut Feeling to Spreadsheet: How Data Changed Football Scouting
articles.teaser: Scouts once relied on long drives and sharp eyes – now the search for the next star often starts on a laptop.
articles.text:
For most of football history, finding new players was a very personal business. Scouts travelled from stadium to stadium, stood in the rain at youth matches and wrote notes about a player's pace, technique and attitude. Their recommendations were based on experience and, to a large extent, on gut feeling. Some scouts were brilliant at this, but the system had obvious weaknesses: nobody can watch every match, and even experts see what they expect to see.

Over the last two decades, this has changed dramatically. Today, almost every professional match is recorded and analysed in detail. Companies collect data on every pass, sprint, tackle and shot, and they sell this information to clubs. As a result, a club can now compare hundreds of players from different leagues without sending anyone on a plane. A small club in one country can identify an underrated defender playing in a league that its scouts have never visited.

The key idea is to measure things that traditional statistics missed. Goals and assists are easy to count, but they do not tell the whole story. Modern analysts look at metrics such as expected goals, which estimates how likely a shot was to go in, or how often a player moves the ball forward into dangerous areas. A midfielder who rarely scores may turn out to be one of the most valuable players on the pitch because he consistently breaks through the opponent's lines.

For clubs with limited budgets, this has been a real opportunity. Instead of competing with rich clubs for famous stars, they can look for players whose value the market has not yet recognised. They buy them relatively cheaply, develop them and often sell them later for a much higher fee. This business model has helped several smaller clubs punch above their weight, both on the pitch and financially.

Still, data has not made human scouts disappear. Numbers can show what a player does, but not always why. They cannot easily measure whether a young player will cope with pressure, adapt to a new country or fit into the dressing room. Statistics from a weaker league may also be misleading, since a player who dominates there might struggle against stronger opponents. That is why most clubs now combine both approaches: data helps them build a shortlist, and scouts then watch the players in person to fill in the gaps.

Interestingly, fans have joined this revolution too. Fantasy football players and online communities discuss advanced statistics that were once known only to professionals. Many supporters now argue about a striker's expected goals as passionately as they once argued about his haircut. In that sense, data has not only changed how clubs find talent – it has also changed how we all talk about the game.
keypoints: Traditionally, scouts travelled to matches and relied on experience and gut feeling, which had limits.
Today most matches are recorded and analysed, so clubs can compare many players from different leagues.
Modern metrics like expected goals measure contributions that simple statistics such as goals miss.
Smaller clubs use data to find undervalued players, develop them and sell them for profit.

articles.title: Between Two Continents: Life on Istanbul's Ferries
articles.teaser: In Istanbul, the daily commute can come with sea views, seagulls and a glass of hot tea.
articles.text:
In most big cities, public transport is something people simply put up with. They squeeze into crowded trains, stare at their phones and count the minutes until they arrive. In Istanbul, one form of transport is different. For many residents, the ferry is not just a way to get to work – it is one of the best parts of the day.

The reason lies in the city's unusual geography. Istanbul is divided by the Bosphorus, a narrow strait that connects the Black Sea with the Sea of Marmara. One side of the city lies in Europe, the other in Asia. Although there are bridges and tunnels today, ferries have linked the two shores for a very long time, and millions of people still depend on them. Every day, boats cross between neighbourhoods on both sides, as well as to the islands in the Sea of Marmara.

A ferry journey has its own rituals. Passengers often buy a glass of black tea and a simit, the round sesame bread that is sold almost everywhere in the city. Regular commuters have their favourite seats: some prefer the warm inside cabin in winter, while others stand at the back to throw bits of bread to the seagulls that follow the boat. On a sunny evening, the crossing offers views of mosques, palaces and old wooden houses along the water that many tourists pay a lot of money to see.

The ferries also shape the rhythm of the city. Because departures run on fixed timetables, people plan their day around them. Friends arrange to meet at a certain pier, and a missed boat can mean waiting twenty minutes for the next one. Neighbourhoods around the main piers have become busy centres full of cafés, fish restaurants and markets. In a sense, the ferry network has helped decide where people live, work and spend their free time.

For visitors, taking a local ferry is one of the easiest and cheapest ways to experience Istanbul like a resident. Instead of booking an expensive tourist cruise, you can use a normal travel card and join commuters on their daily route. You will hear conversations in Turkish, see students doing homework and watch business people in suits enjoying a quiet moment before a busy day.

Of course, the city keeps changing. New metro lines and roads offer faster options, and traffic on the water has to compete with them. Yet many people in Istanbul say they would never give up their ferry. Perhaps that is because the short trip between two continents offers something rare in a big city: a moment to breathe, look around and remember where you are.
keypoints: For many Istanbul residents, the ferry is an enjoyable part of the day, not just transport.
The Bosphorus divides the city between Europe and Asia, and ferries have long connected both sides.
Ferry trips have rituals like drinking tea, eating simit and feeding seagulls, with beautiful views.
Ferry timetables and piers shape daily routines and have created busy neighbourhoods around the piers.
Tourists can take normal ferries cheaply to experience the city like locals, and many residents value the ferry despite newer transport.

articles.title: Why We Put Things Off – and What Actually Helps
articles.teaser: Procrastination is not really about laziness, and understanding that might be the first step to beating it.
articles.text:
Almost everyone knows the feeling. There is an important report to write, a tax form to complete or a difficult email to answer. Instead of starting, you check your phone, clean your desk or suddenly decide that the kitchen needs reorganising. Hours later, the task is still waiting, and now you also feel guilty. Why do we do this, even when we know it makes our lives harder?

For a long time, procrastination was seen as a problem of poor time management or simple laziness. Many psychologists now believe this view is wrong. According to a growing body of research, procrastination is mainly about emotions. We do not avoid tasks because we have no time, but because the task makes us feel bad. It might be boring, confusing or stressful, or we might be afraid of doing it badly. Putting it off gives us quick relief from these unpleasant feelings.

The problem is that this relief is only short-term. Our brains are very good at choosing what feels good now over what is good for us later. Researchers sometimes describe this as a conflict between our present self and our future self. The present self wants comfort; the future self has to deal with the deadline, the stress and the lower-quality work. Interestingly, some studies suggest that people think about their future self almost like a stranger, which makes it easier to leave problems for "someone else".

So what actually helps? One common piece of advice is to make the first step very small. Instead of "write the report", the goal becomes "open the document and write one sentence". Once people get started, the task often feels less threatening, and they continue. Another method is to set a timer for a short period, for example twenty-five minutes, and promise yourself a break afterwards.

It also helps to change the environment. If your phone is on the desk, it will win the battle for your attention. Putting it in another room removes the temptation. Some people find it useful to tell a colleague or friend about their plan, because being accountable to someone else increases the pressure to follow through.

Finally, experts recommend being kind to yourself. It may sound strange, but people who criticise themselves harshly after procrastinating often procrastinate more next time, because the task now feels even worse. Forgiving yourself and simply starting again tends to be more effective. Procrastination is a very human habit, not a sign of weak character – and like most habits, it can be changed step by step.
keypoints: Procrastination means avoiding important tasks, and it often leaves people feeling guilty.
Many psychologists think procrastination is about managing bad emotions, not laziness or poor time management.
Delaying brings short-term relief, but the present self chooses comfort at the cost of the future self.
Helpful strategies include making the first step very small, using timers and removing distractions like phones.

articles.title: What Disaster Movies Get Wrong About Earthquakes
articles.teaser: Giant cracks swallowing cities make great cinema – but the real science is both less dramatic and more surprising.
articles.text:
Few film genres are as spectacular as the disaster movie. Skyscrapers collapse like playing cards, the ground splits open beneath the hero's car and a scientist who nobody believed races against time to save the city. Audiences love it, and the special effects keep getting better. But if you ask seismologists – the scientists who study earthquakes – many of these scenes range from slightly exaggerated to completely impossible.

Take the classic image of the earth opening up into a huge, bottomless gap that swallows cars and people. In real earthquakes, the ground can crack, and landslides can cause serious damage. However, faults do not usually open into deep chasms. An earthquake happens when two blocks of rock suddenly slide past each other along a fault. The movement is mostly sideways or up and down, and the enormous pressure deep underground keeps the rock pressed together. A giant canyon appearing in the middle of a city is pure Hollywood.

Another common myth is that scientists can predict exactly when and where a big earthquake will strike. In many films, the hero reads a strange pattern on a computer screen and warns that a disaster will happen in a few hours. In reality, no reliable method exists to predict earthquakes in this way. What researchers can do is estimate the probability of a strong earthquake in a region over several decades. Some countries also have early warning systems, but these work only after an earthquake has already started, giving people a few seconds – perhaps enough to stop trains or take cover under a table.

Films also tend to exaggerate the size of earthquakes. Scripts sometimes invent magnitudes far beyond anything that has ever been recorded, often caused by one enormous fault running across an entire continent. The size of an earthquake depends largely on the length of the fault that breaks, and there are physical limits to how long faults can be. Real earthquakes are terrible enough without these inventions.

Interestingly, what films often get wrong is not only the drama but also the human reaction. Disaster movies love scenes of mass panic, with crowds running wildly through the streets. Research on real disasters suggests that people usually behave more calmly and helpfully than we expect. Neighbours dig each other out of rubble, and strangers share food and shelter long before official help arrives.

None of this means you should stop enjoying disaster movies. They are entertainment, not documentaries. But the real lessons are worth remembering: earthquakes cannot be predicted to the hour, buildings designed to modern standards save lives, and knowing what to do – drop to the ground, take cover and hold on – matters far more than a heroic last-minute escape.
keypoints: Disaster movies are spectacular, but seismologists say many earthquake scenes are exaggerated or impossible.
The ground does not usually open into huge chasms, because rocks slide past each other and are pressed together.
Scientists cannot predict the exact time of an earthquake; they can only estimate long-term probabilities, and warning systems give only seconds.
Films exaggerate earthquake size, but the magnitude is limited by the length of the fault.
In real disasters people are usually calm and helpful, and good buildings and knowing how to react matter most.

articles.topic_de: Widersprechen in Meetings über Kulturen hinweg
articles.title: The Art of Saying No: Disagreeing in Meetings Across Cultures
articles.teaser: What sounds like honest feedback in one country can come across as a personal attack in another.
articles.text:
Picture a video call with colleagues from four countries. A project manager presents a plan, and a German participant replies, "I don't think this will work – the timeline is unrealistic." To him, this is simply a useful contribution. To a colleague from a culture where open criticism is handled with far more care, it may have sounded almost rude. Meanwhile, a third participant said, "That's an interesting idea, perhaps we could look at it again later," and everyone who shares her background knows that this was, in fact, a firm no.

Moments like these illustrate one of the trickiest aspects of international business. Cultures differ not only in whether people disagree, but in how openly they do so. Researchers who study workplace communication often place cultures on a spectrum. At one end are those where direct disagreement is seen as a sign of engagement and honesty; confronting an idea, the logic goes, is not the same as confronting the person. At the other end are cultures that prize harmony and face-saving, where disagreement is expressed indirectly, softened with polite phrases or saved for a private conversation after the meeting.

Neither approach is inherently better, and each has its blind spots. Direct communicators risk damaging relationships and silencing colleagues who are uncomfortable arguing in public. Indirect communicators, on the other hand, risk having their concerns overlooked altogether, particularly by listeners who take every word at face value. In mixed teams, the result can be a frustrating spiral: one side feels attacked, the other feels ignored, and important problems remain unspoken until it is too late.

So how can professionals navigate this minefield? A good starting point is to become aware of your own default style and to recognise that it is a cultural habit rather than a universal standard. From there, small adjustments go a long way. Direct speakers can use "downgraders" – phrases such as "I wonder whether" or "I'm slightly concerned that" – which soften the message without hiding it. Separating the idea from its author also helps: acknowledging what is useful about a proposal before raising doubts shows respect while still putting the problem on the table.

Listeners have a role to play, too. In international meetings, it pays to read between the lines and to notice what is not being said. A long pause or a vague "we will consider it" may deserve a follow-up question. Leaders can make disagreement safer by asking for concerns explicitly, inviting written feedback or speaking to quieter team members one-on-one.

Ultimately, the goal is not for everyone to adopt the same style but to build a shared understanding of how the team communicates. Some teams even agree on explicit ground rules at the start of a project. It may feel awkward at first, yet it is far less awkward than discovering, months later, that half the room never agreed with the plan in the first place.
keypoints: People from different cultures disagree in meetings in different ways, which can cause misunderstandings.
Cultures lie on a spectrum from direct disagreement, seen as honest, to indirect disagreement that protects harmony and face.
Neither style is better: direct speakers can damage relationships, while indirect speakers' concerns may be overlooked.
Speakers can adapt by knowing their own style, using softening phrases and separating the idea from the person.
Listeners and leaders should read between the lines and invite concerns, and teams can agree on shared communication rules.
